BreakingUpdated 5:25 a.m. ET Tuesday

Chow begins second term pledging tax hikes near inflation, a TTC fare cap and 10,000 rental starts

Latest CTV News · Tue 5:05 a.m.First reported by CP24 and CTV News · Mon 9:59 p.m.

Re-elected with about 54 per cent, Olivia Chow has promised to keep property tax increases at or around inflation, cap TTC fares after 10 rides a week and start 10,000 rental homes in 2027 (CTV News). She will lead a progressive, new-look council that includes her allies Nate Erskine-Smith and Mike Layton (CBC News). Elsewhere, Keanin Loomis ousted Hamilton’s Andrea Horwath, Alvin Tedjo unseated Carolyn Parrish in Mississauga and Milton’s Gord Krantz lost after 46 years (Global News).

  • 529,042 votes for Chow (54.17%) to 401,415 for Bradford (41.11%), with 1,420 of 1,431 polls in, in the City of Toronto’s unofficial results (City of Toronto)
  • 976,550 votes cast for Toronto mayor with 99.2% of polls in, up from 563,124 in 2022; Chow won 19 of 25 wards, including all five in Scarborough (CTV News)
  • 74,479 votes (39.2%) for Tedjo in Mississauga, to 51,853 (27.3%) for Parrish and 43,191 (22.7%) for Bonnie Crombie (CBC News)
  • 41.77% for Keanin Loomis in Hamilton, to 31.87% for Coun. Rob Cooper and 14.53% for Mayor Andrea Horwath; eight new councillors, and turnout of 31.59%, down from 35.58%, unofficial results show (CBC News)
  • 16,112 votes for Minakakis in Milton to 8,878 for Krantz, mayor since 1980, with 31 of 38 polls reporting (insauga)
  • 44.6% for Sutcliffe in Ottawa to 33.9% for Jeff Leiper; turnout 36.2% (CTV News)
  • Kingston’s official results, which the city says will be posted Tuesday; unofficial results give Conny Glenn 43.25 per cent to 41.17 for Mayor Bryan Paterson, a 793-vote margin (The Queen’s Journal); Glenn’s term begins when the new council is sworn in Nov. 15 (The Queen’s Journal)
  • Final results: Toronto’s are unofficial, and the City Clerk is expected to certify them later in the week (Global News)
  • Sudbury’s final count: as of 3 a.m. the city had not updated results, with about 14,000 paper ballots to count; Mayor Paul Lefebvre had 25,889 votes (about 63 per cent) to 11,105 for Miranda Rocca-Circelli in the tally so far (CBC News)

What we know

  • CP24 and CTV News were first to declare Chow’s victory, at 9:59 p.m. “Whether you voted for me or voted for someone else … I am your mayor too,” she said (CTV News). Toronto is “a progressive city, a city of compassion, a city that welcome newcomers,” she said (Global News). “I will never stop listening, never stop fighting, never stop caring for the people of our city” (CBC News).
  • Bradford conceded: “She is the mayor of this city. Nobody can doubt that” (CTV News).
  • Chow ran on affordability, with promises to freeze TTC fares and make transit free after 10 paid rides a week (CTV News).
  • Loomis, former head of the Hamilton Chamber of Commerce, lost to Horwath by about 1,600 votes in 2022 and beat her by more than 35,000 on Monday (CTV News).
  • Marianne Meed Ward was re-elected in Burlington (CHCH); Steven Del Duca won Vaughan with 81.5 per cent, the city’s website shows (CBC News).
  • Elsewhere: Patrick Brown won a third term in Brampton (insauga); Conny Glenn beat incumbent Bryan Paterson in Kingston (Global News); Michael Eamon won Peterborough (Global News); Fred Francis beat Drew Dilkens in Windsor (CBC News); Berry Vrbanovic won a fourth term in Kitchener (CBC News). Josh Morgan was re-elected in London (CBC News); four Waterloo region mayors lost, including Waterloo’s Dorothy McCabe and Cambridge’s Jan Liggett (CBC News).

Not yet known

  • Toronto’s official turnout; preliminary results show more than 45 per cent voted for mayor (Toronto Star).
  • Final, certified results in every city (Global News).
Confirmation tracker 15 outlets

Verified: unofficial results posted by the City of Toronto, reported by CTV News and CP24, CBC News, Global News, CityNews, the Toronto Star, the National Post, the Toronto Sun, The Hamilton Spectator, CHCH, insauga, Radio-Canada, Global News Kingston, CBC Sudbury and The Canadian Press.

Canada and the U.S.Developing

Carney says the U.S. is ‘coming closer to our position’ as trade talks gain momentum, but he can’t guarantee Trump will honour a deal

“Canada’s ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians … with very clear bottom lines, red lines,” Carney said Monday after a meeting of First Nations leaders and first ministers in Ottawa; asked how he knows Trump will sign in pen, he said, “I don’t know that.” Government and industry sources told CTV News the White House has considerable appetite for a deal before next week’s midterms (CTV News). Last week, the U.S. Embassy’s fact sheet listed remarks by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and others as attempts to influence the Nov. 3 vote; Carney replied that the U.S. “initiated a series of trade actions” and Ford said he has “no interest at all interfering in American elections” (CBC News). It names 11 people charged or sentenced for illegally voting in U.S. elections but gives no evidence tying them to Ottawa (Al Jazeera). Carney says he spoke with Trump Wednesday morning and “did address some of the issues around trade” (CTV News); former president Bill Clinton said of Trump’s treatment of Canada, “I’m tired of treating our allies like they’re dirt” (CTV News).

    Smaller newsrooms

    Today’s top five from independent and northern newsrooms, with an eye on the Arctic. Updated Monday morning.

    1. Nunatsiaq NewsNunavut Arctic

      Nunavut teachers feeling the strain as student support workers disappear

      Federal Inuit Child First money no longer covers most school requests, so classrooms have fewer support assistants this year and teachers report burnout. Ottawa has extended the program a year with a $115-million top-up and now reviews school requests case by case.

      By Miriam Lafontaine
    2. Yellowknifer (NNSL)Nunavut Arctic

      Coast Guard’s only large drone put through Arctic trials in Iqaluit

      The Canadian Coast Guard is testing its lone Hermes 900 surveillance drone out of Iqaluit until spring 2027, for jobs like tracking ships, spotting pollution and scouting ice.

      By William Koblensky Varela, Local Journalism Initiative
    3. Nunatsiaq NewsNunavut Arctic

      Qikiqtarjuaq man loses his jury trial after sleeping through its start

      About 60 prospective jurors turned out in September. A judge ruled oversleeping was no excuse, so the sexual assault trial resumes before a judge alone in February.

      By Miriam Lafontaine
    4. The TyeeBritish Columbia

      Incumbent mayors swept out across B.C., Kamloops included

      Kamloops Mayor Reid Hamer-Jackson finished fourth, and sitting mayors also lost in Surrey, Langley, West Vancouver, Quesnel and Penticton.

      By Tyler Olsen
    5. Yukon NewsYukon Arctic

      Yukon’s mid-year budget update shows restraint, for now

      Columnist Keith Halliday says the supplementary budget trims the deficit slightly and keeps public-service staffing nearly flat, but a costly union contract and shaky bond markets could undo it.

      By Keith Halliday

    Canada and the U.S.

    Where the trade war stands, what changed this week, and what comes next. Every line links to the newsroom that reported it. Updated Tuesday, Oct. 27, 4:32 a.m. ET.

    Trade talksNo formal talks since Aug. 22; contacts picking upCarney said Monday there has been a “slight, slight intensification” of talks and that any progress is “because the U.S. is coming closer to our position,” but there is no deal and he cannot be sure Trump would honour one: asked if Trump would sign in pen, he said, “I don’t know that” (CTV News, The Associated Press). White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News on Sunday the two sides are “very close” to a deal (Bloomberg, CTV News); Trump told a Michigan rally the trade war would end “pretty soon” (Global News (Canadian Press)). Canada–U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office says Canada remains in “constructive dialogue” with Washington (AP). Sources say the two sides are working on a deal to ease U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, with LeBlanc and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in regular contact (Reuters); political-level talks are “moving quickly,” but formal talks between negotiators have not begun and sources doubt a deal before the Nov. 3 midterms (Global News). Several Canadian sources told CBC News and Radio-Canada the gap between the sides has been too wide in recent days to reach an agreement, and one said, “We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet” (CBC News, Radio-Canada).
    50%U.S. tariff on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol and hockey gear. In force since Aug. 22. On Oct. 30, plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery come off the list and items such as valves, carpets and waste products go on.White House (fact sheet) · The Associated Press · NPR · The Hill
    15–50%Canada’s counter-tariffs on nearly $20 billion of U.S. goods, more than 700 products, from steel to appliances. In force since Sept. 8.Al Jazeera · CNBC
    ~35%Total U.S. duty on Canadian softwood lumber after the Commerce Department’s latest review, the BC Lumber Trade Council says. Set Oct. 14.CTV News · CBC News
    AnnualCUSMA review. The U.S. declined on July 1 to extend the trade deal for 16 years, so it now faces a review every year.CBC News · National Observer
    $9BJoint Ottawa–Ontario plan for sectors hit by U.S. tariffs: $5 billion for a steel action fund, $2.5 billion for autos, and Ring of Fire roads. Announced Oct. 21.Castanet (Canadian Press) · Canadian HR Reporter · Bloomberg (subscribers)

    How U.S. media see Canada

    American coverage since Friday has framed Trump’s changes to the Canada tariff list mainly through the U.S. midterms, especially Sen. Susan Collins’s close race in Maine: AP said Trump was “seeking to help” Collins (AP), Maine’s Bangor Daily News reported the change came after a Wall Street Journal report that it was meant to aid her re-election (Bangor Daily News), and outlets on the right and left, from Townhall to AlterNet, cast it as a political move (Townhall, AlterNet). By Monday the focus had moved to whether a deal is near, with Fox Business and Bloomberg highlighting Hassett’s “very close” (Fox Business, Bloomberg) and AP setting Carney’s claim of progress against his doubts Trump would honour a deal (AP). Here is what American newsrooms are telling their readers about Canada, newest first.

    • The Associated PressNews agencyMon Oct. 26Carney says Trump moving closer to Canada’s trade demands as midterms loomRob Gillies anchors the story in Carney’s claim of a “slight, slight intensification” of talks, then sets it against his doubts that Trump would honour a deal and Trump’s own mixed timeline, “pretty soon” or months. It notes that energy accounts for most of the U.S. trade deficit with Canada. Carried by The Washington Post (subscribers), ABC News , WSOC-TV Charlotte and The Washington Times.
    • Fox BusinessBusiness newsMon Oct. 26Canada trade deal ‘very close’ as President Trump adjusts tariffsThe business network’s video segment centres on Hassett’s optimism that a final agreement is coming soon, with trade expert Samir Kapadia weighing the new tariff exemptions.
    • BloombergBusiness newsSun Oct. 25Hassett says US-Canada trade talks are ‘very close’ to dealMaría Paula Mijares Torres leads with the White House adviser’s Fox News remark that the two sides are “very close” and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick “has been talking to his Canadian counterparts all week.” Carried by The Spokesman-Review.
    • Fox NewsTV networkSat Oct. 24Canada is feeling the pain from Trump’s tariffs, but the trade fight didn’t start overnightAmanda Macias presents the tariffs as hurting Canadian industry and households, with steel exports down sharply and prices rising, and frames the fight as a long-running dispute over dairy access and lumber rather than a sudden break; analysts quoted urge both countries to preserve the relationship.
    • The Associated PressNews agencyFri Oct. 23Trump, seeking to help Maine Sen. Susan Collins, exempts some Canadian imports from his 50% tariffsPaul Wiseman frames the exemptions as help for Collins in a tight race, set against voters’ cost-of-living worries; he cites an AP-NORC poll in which 65% blame Trump’s policies more than outside factors for high prices, and Sen. Ron Wyden calling the move “an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies.” Carried by Cox Media stations including KIRO 7 Seattle and WFTV Orlando.
    • Bangor Daily NewsNewspaperFri Oct. 23Donald Trump to lift some Canadian tariffsEthan Andrews and Michael Shepherd tell the story through Maine’s Senate race: the exemptions target blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers, and Democrat Troy Jackson says he won’t credit Collins for removing a few items “when we should have never had a list.”
    • TownhallNews siteFri Oct. 23The Tariffs Against Canada Just Changed: Here’s What to KnowCameron Arcand, at the conservative site, explains what comes off and goes on the list, cites the Journal’s report that the move is meant to help Collins, and quotes the White House: Trump “continues to address Canada’s discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce.”
    • AlterNetNews siteFri Oct. 23Trump raises eyebrows with ‘Hail Mary’ pass to save Collins’ hideNick Hilden, at the progressive site, casts the rollback as a last-minute gamble to rescue Collins, and notes Republicans in Michigan and New Hampshire are also distancing themselves from the tariffs.

    This week

    1. Mon Oct. 26

      Sources: the U.S. and Canada are working on a deal to ease steel and auto tariffs. Two U.S. and four Canadian sources told Reuters the talks concern Section 232 tariffs of up to 50% on Canadian steel and 25% on autos, run by the Commerce Department, so Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is central; he and LeBlanc are in regular contact. One Canadian source said a deal before Nov. 3 is possible; a U.S. source said Washington wants more concessions, and an industry source expects any deal to be “narrowed.” Global News sources say political-level talks are “moving quickly” but doubt a deal before the midterms, and formal talks between negotiators have not begun. A source told Radio-Canada there are “substantive conversations, but there are still key elements that remain unresolved,” and several Canadian sources told CBC News the gap has been too wide in recent days for an agreement; chief negotiator Janice Charette said last week, “Pens are down, and the doors are open.”

      Reuters (via Investing.com) · Global News · CBC News · Radio-Canada
    2. Mon Oct. 26

      Carney: the U.S. is “coming closer to our position.” Speaking in Ottawa after a meeting of First Nations leaders and first ministers, Carney said talks have seen a “slight, slight intensification” but Canada’s position is unchanged, and that it is ready to sign a deal with “very clear bottom lines, red lines.” He said he can’t guarantee Trump would respect an agreement. LeBlanc’s office says Canada remains in “constructive dialogue.”

      BNN Bloomberg (CTV News) · The Associated Press · Bloomberg (subscribers)
    3. Sun Oct. 25

      Trump at a Port Huron, Mich., rally: Canada is “willing to give us anything at this moment.” He said the trade war would be settled “pretty soon” and that Canada “has been ripping off the United States for years,” The Canadian Press reports. Earlier Sunday, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News the countries are “very close” to a deal, Bloomberg reports; CTV News says he also blamed Alberta’s referendum for making talks “essentially impossible.” Government and industry sources told CTV News there is “considerable appetite from the White House to strike a deal with Canada.”

      Global News (Canadian Press) · CTV News · The Spokesman-Review (Bloomberg) · CTV News (Hassett) · CTV News (sources)
    4. Fri Oct. 23

      Trump reshuffles the 50% tariff list. Carney: “We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there.” A proclamation signed Friday takes plywood sheets, packing crates, some paper products and some machinery and refrigeration equipment off the list, and adds items including valves, carpets and waste products, from Oct. 30, the White House says; CTV News reports cocoa powder, vinyl flooring and shampoos are also added. Maine Sen. Susan Collins said she secured the exemptions for blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers. LeBlanc’s office said Canada will assess the measures and “stands ready to work constructively.” Trump said Canada is “working very hard to make a deal” and “we have all the cards.”

      BNN Bloomberg (CTV News) · CP24 (CTV News) · The Associated Press · White House (fact sheet) · Bangor Daily News
    5. Thu Oct. 22

      Ottawa tells its diplomats in the U.S. not to meet midterm candidates. A Global Affairs Canada memo sent Tuesday asks for “a very risk-averse approach” given “heightened sensitivity,” after the U.S. embassy’s interference accusations, The Canadian Press reports. In Istanbul on Friday, Carney said the claims had “no merit” and that he was disappointed the U.S. ambassador saw it as his role to make them.

      CP24 (Canadian Press) · Castanet (Canadian Press) · CTV News
    6. Thu Oct. 22

      Carney arrives in Turkey, the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister, as he looks beyond the U.S. for trade. He laid a wreath at Atatürk’s mausoleum on arrival, and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan welcomed him at the Presidential Complex in Ankara on Thursday, Daily Sabah reports; he meets business leaders in Istanbul on Friday, with Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson along, The Canadian Press reports. A former Turkish ambassador to Canada told CP both countries need alternatives to the “increasingly protectionist U.S. market.” Reuters says the visit is part of Carney’s push to deepen trade with other “middle powers” and reduce dependence on the U.S., which still takes nearly 70% of Canada’s exports; Turkey accounts for less than 0.3% of Canada’s merchandise trade. Canada’s ambassador told AP the aim is to “launch a strategic partnership through a joint declaration by the two leaders,” with talks on energy, nuclear plants, mining, defence and a free-trade agreement.

      CP24 (Canadian Press) · iNFOnews (Canadian Press) · Al-Monitor (Reuters) · CBC News · The Associated Press · Daily Sabah
    7. Wed Oct. 21

      U.S. embassy accuses Canadian politicians of trying to “influence American politics.” The embassy released a list of quotes it says show such plans, The Canadian Press reports; Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is quoted five times, in remarks taken from Canada’s response to U.S. tariffs, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford is also on it. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra says the U.S. is “closely watching.” Carney did not directly address the accusations, noting the U.S. started the trade actions; Ford said he has no interest in interfering in American elections. The embassy’s fact sheet also names Liberal MP Anthony Housefather and Consul General Bernadette Jordan, and ends: “Americans decide America’s elections.” The embassy also cited Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections since 2012, but provided no evidence linking those cases to the Canadian government, AP reports; more than 275,000 people have signed a parliamentary petition calling for Hoekstra’s removal. Separately, the embassy told The Maple, in a statement it said was cleared by the State Department, that “there will not be a future meeting” between State Department staff and Alberta separatists.

      CBC News · Al Jazeera · U.S. Embassy (fact sheet) · CP24 (Canadian Press) · BNN Bloomberg (Canadian Press) · CBC News · The Maple · The Associated Press

    What comes next

    1. Thu Oct. 29–Fri Oct. 30

      Canada–EU summit in Montreal. Carney hosts European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who has proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member, AP reports.

      Global Affairs Canada · The Associated Press
    2. Fri Oct. 30

      Changes to the 50% U.S. tariff list take effect. Plywood sheets, packing crates and some machinery come off; valves, carpets, waste products and others go on.

      White House (fact sheet) · The Associated Press · BNN Bloomberg (CTV News)
    3. Tue Nov. 3

      U.S. midterms. Maine and Michigan, both tied closely to Canada, have competitive races. Sen. Susan Collins, in a toss-up race, won tariff exemptions for Maine producers on Oct. 23, and Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers says “we need to end this tariff war now.” Canadian officials told industry groups last week they did not expect a deal before the vote, CBC News reported; Trump said Sunday a deal might come before the midterms, or take months, AP reports.

      The Associated Press · CBC News · Atlantic Council · Inside U.S. Trade
    4. Thu Nov. 5

      Federal budget, two days after the U.S. midterms. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced the date in question period on Tuesday, with U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariffs still in force.

      Global News · CBC News
    5. Fri Jan. 1, 2027

      Threatened 50% U.S. tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks and auto parts. Trump said in August, after talks collapsed, that the tariffs would start Jan. 1, with “ZERO TARIFFS” for companies that build in the U.S. CBC News described the threat as looming in its Oct. 20 report on the stalled talks.

      CBC News · CNBC · CBS News · Al Jazeera
    6. Watching

      Oil and autos. Oil has been spared so far. The average tariff on Canadian autos and parts rose from 0.2% in February 2025 to 9.2% this August.

      Atlantic Council

      About Palindrome

      How we work, where our news comes from, and how to reach us.

      Methodology

      A story gets a full Palindrome summary only when six independent newsrooms have reported it. Outlets with the same owner count as one.

      Until then it runs as developing news, with a meter showing how many outlets have it. Breaking news can run sooner, credited to the outlet that reported it, and is labelled unconfirmed.

      Every summary links to the reporting it draws on. Tapping a story takes you to the newest, fullest report, and each story credits the outlet that reported it first: the earliest report we found.
